section: Where this chapter sits in the course
text:
Where this chapter sits in the course
Chapter 1 described light as a wave, Chapter 2 guided it in fibers, Chapter 3 built the pn junction and the LED, and Chapter 4 the laser and the optical amplifier. Chapter 5 closes the link: the photodetector converts the optical power back into an electrical current. It uses the same pn junction as the LED of Ch. 3, run in reverse: a photon of energy \(h\nu>E_g\) creates an electron–hole pair, the field of the depletion region separates it, and a current flows in the external circuit. Three questions organise the chapter:

How many electrons per photon? Absorption coefficient, quantum efficiency, responsivity, and internal gain (avalanche photodiodes, photoconductors, phototransistors).
How fast? Drift and diffusion of the carriers (the Shockley–Ramo theorem), transit time, and the \(RC\) constant of the junction capacitance and the load.
How weak a signal? Shot noise, thermal noise, excess avalanche noise, SNR, NEP and detectivity, which set the sensitivity of every fiber receiver (Ch. 2) and the noise floor that the EDFA of Ch. 4 must beat.

The same physics then makes image sensors (CCD and CMOS arrays of photodiodes) and, in forward bias with a load, solar cells.

title: 1  The pn junction photodiode
text:
1.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 4–9 (reverse-biased, shorted and open-circuit pn junction under light, drift and diffusion of photogenerated carriers) and 10 (sign conventions, the I–V characteristic in the dark and under illumination, photodiode and photovoltaic modes).
A photon with \(h\nu>E_g\) absorbed in a semiconductor creates an electron–hole pair (EHP). If it is created in the depletion region (space-charge layer, SCL) of a pn junction, the built-in field \(E_o\) separates the pair at once: the electron rolls down \(E_c\) to the n side and the hole rolls up \(E_v\) to the p side (slide 6). If it is created in a neutral region, the minority carrier must first diffuse to the SCL; it is collected only if it gets there before it recombines, i.e. within about one diffusion length \(L_e\) or \(L_h\) (slide 7, Ch. 3).
Each collected pair moves one electron charge around the external circuit. The photodiode is therefore a current source \(I_{ph}\) in parallel with the ordinary diode of Ch. 3. With the sign convention of slide 10 (positive \(I\) and \(V\) as in forward bias),
\[
I=I_o\left[\exp\!\left(\frac{eV}{\eta k_BT}\right)-1\right]-I_{ph},\qquad I_{ph}=\mathcal{R}P_o ,
\]
where \(\mathcal R\) is the responsivity (Chapter 4). The illuminated curve is the dark curve shifted down by \(I_{ph}\). Three operating points matter:
\[
V_{oc}=\frac{\eta k_BT}{e}\ln\!\left(1+\frac{I_{ph}}{I_o}\right).
\]
With a load the photodiode delivers power: this is the photovoltaic mode of the solar cell (Chapter 13).

title: 1  The pn junction photodiode
text:
Reverse bias (\(V=-V_r\), third quadrant): \(I\approx-I_{ph}-I_o\), a current proportional to the power. This is the photodiode (photoconductive) mode used for detection: linear, fast (wide SCL, small capacitance), but with a dark current.
Short circuit (\(V=0\)): \(I_{sc}=-I_{ph}\) (slide 8). Still linear, and no bias means almost no dark current.
Open circuit (\(I=0\), fourth quadrant): the separated carriers charge the n side negative and the p side positive. This forward voltage lowers the barrier until diffusion back across the junction cancels the photocurrent (slide 9):

The reverse-biased photodiode is a linear power meter; the open-circuit photodiode is a logarithmic one. The first is the basis of every optical receiver; the second is useful for wide-dynamic-range light meters and is the operating principle of the solar cell.






TipGoing further






Where is the dark current coming from? In reverse bias \(I_o\) has a diffusion part \(\propto n_i^2\) and a generation part in the SCL \(\propto n_iW/\tau_g\) (Ch. 3). Which dominates in Si at room temperature, and how does each scale with temperature and band gap? Estimate the increase of the dark current of a Si photodiode between 25 °C and 75 °C.
Zero-bias (photovoltaic-mode) detection is used in precision photometry: there is no dark current, only the thermal (Johnson) noise of the shunt resistance \(R_p=\eta k_BT/eI_o\). Compute \(R_p\) for \(I_o=10\) pA and compare its noise with the shot noise of 10 pA in reverse bias (Chapter 10).
Photon recycling in the neutral regions. The collection probability of a carrier generated at a distance \(x\) from the SCL is \(\approx e^{-x/L}\). Combine it with \(e^{-\alpha x}\) to obtain the internal QE of a pn photodiode (Chapter 4).

title: 2  The Shockley–Ramo theorem
text:
2.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 11–15 (induced current of a photogenerated electron–hole pair drifting between two electrodes, electron and hole transit times, total collected charge).
When does the external current flow: when the carriers reach the electrodes, or while they move? The Shockley–Ramo theorem answers: while they move. Consider an EHP created at \(x=l\) in a semiconductor of length \(L\) between two electrodes held at a voltage \(V\), with a uniform field \(E=V/L\) (slide 11). In a time \(dt\) the electron drifts \(dx=v_edt\) and the field does the work \(eE\,dx\) on it. That energy comes from the battery, which supplies \(Vi_e(t)dt\) (slide 12):
\[
eE\,dx=Vi_e\,dt\quad\Longrightarrow\quad i_e(t)=\frac{ev_e}{L}\quad (t<t_e),\qquad i_h(t)=\frac{ev_h}{L}\quad (t<t_h),
\]
with the transit times \(t_e=(L-l)/v_e\) and \(t_h=l/v_h\) (slide 14). Each carrier gives a rectangular current pulse. Neither pulse alone carries a full electron charge, but together they do (slide 15):
\[
Q=\int_0^{t_e}i_e\,dt+\int_0^{t_h}i_h\,dt=e\frac{L-l}{L}+e\frac{l}{L}=e .
\]
The current starts as soon as the pair is created, not when the first carrier arrives. The duration of the pulse, set by the slowest carrier that has the longest way to go, is the transit-time limit of the detector speed (Chapter 5).

TipGoing further






The general theorem. For any electrode geometry, a charge \(q\) moving with velocity \(\mathbf v\) induces on electrode \(k\) the current \(i_k=q\,\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf E_w\), where \(\mathbf E_w\) is the weighting field: the field obtained with electrode \(k\) at 1 V, all others grounded and all charges removed. For parallel plates \(E_w=1/L\) and we recover slide 12. In an interdigitated MSM detector (Chapter 7) \(E_w\) is concentrated near the fingers: a carrier contributes most of its current when it is close to the electrode. Compute \(E_w\) for a pixelated X-ray detector and explain the “small-pixel effect”.
Uni-travelling-carrier (UTC) photodiode. Absorb the light in a thin p-doped layer, where the photogenerated holes are majority carriers and relax immediately; only electrons enter the depleted collector, at velocities up to \(3\times10^5\) m/s in InP (velocity overshoot). UTC photodiodes reach > 100 GHz and high saturation currents (no hole pile-up). Use the panel with the hole velocity set very high to mimic it.
Space charge. At high photocurrents the drifting carriers screen the field (the photocurrent density approaches \(\varepsilon v_{sat}V/W^2\)) and the response saturates. Estimate this saturation current for a 20 µm diameter, 1 µm thick InGaAs pin at 3 V.

title: 3  Absorption and the cut-off wavelength
text:
3.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 16 (absorption coefficient and penetration depth), 17 and 19 (direct and indirect transitions, phonon-assisted absorption), 18 (cut-off wavelength) and 20 (band gaps and cut-off wavelengths of photodetector materials).
Light entering a semiconductor is absorbed exponentially (Beer–Lambert, slide 16):
\[
I(x)=I_o\,e^{-\alpha x},\qquad \delta=\frac1\alpha\ \text{(penetration depth)},\qquad
\text{fraction absorbed in a thickness }d:\ 1-e^{-\alpha d}.
\]
Band-to-band absorption needs \(h\nu\ge E_g\), which defines the cut-off wavelength (slide 18)
\[
\lambda_g\,[\mu\text{m}]\approx\frac{1.24}{E_g\,[\text{eV}]} .
\]
Momentum must also be conserved. A photon carries almost no momentum (\(\hbar k_\text{photon}\ll\hbar\pi/a\)), so in a direct gap semiconductor (GaAs, InP, InGaAs) the transition is vertical in \(k\) and α rises steeply above \(E_g\), roughly as \(\sqrt{h\nu-E_g}\), to \(10^6\)–\(10^7\) m⁻¹ (slide 17). In an indirect gap semiconductor (Si, Ge) the conduction-band minimum is at a different \(k\): a phonon of wavevector \(K=k_{CB}-k_{VB}\) must be absorbed or emitted (slide 19), so \(h\nu=E_g\pm h\vartheta\) with \(h\vartheta<0.1\) eV. This second-order process is weak: α of Si is only \(10^3\)–\(10^5\) m⁻¹ over the near infrared, and a Si detector for 900 nm must be tens of µm thick. Ge is indirect (\(E_g=0.66\) eV) but has a direct gap at 0.80 eV just above it: its absorption jumps by two orders of magnitude below 1.55 µm (slide 16), which is why Ge photodiodes work at 1550 nm.

title: 4  Quantum efficiency and responsivity
text:
4.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 21–26 (external quantum efficiency, responsivity, the ideal photodiode, maximum QE), 27–28 (internal quantum efficiency and the wavelength dependence of the photocurrent), 33–36 (responsivity of commercial pin photodiodes, effect of the device structure and of temperature, worked example), 139–145 (photocurrent from the device structure, p⁺n versus pin) and 149–150 (Ge photodiode).
The external quantum efficiency counts collected electrons per incident photon, and the responsivity converts it to amperes per watt (slides 21–22):
\[
\eta_e=\frac{I_{ph}/e}{P_o/h\nu},\qquad
\mathcal R=\frac{I_{ph}}{P_o}=\eta_e\frac{e}{h\nu}=\eta_e\frac{e\lambda}{hc}=\eta_e\,\frac{\lambda\,[\mu\text m]}{1.24}\ \text{A/W}.
\]
An ideal photodiode (\(\eta_e=1\)) has \(\mathcal R\) growing linearly with λ up to the cut-off \(\lambda_g\), then falling to zero (slide 24). Real photodiodes lose photons by reflection at the surface (transmission \(T\)), by absorption in regions from which carriers are not collected, and by transmission through the device. With the internal quantum efficiency \(\eta_i\) (pairs per absorbed photon, slide 28) and the useful (collecting) region between \(x_1=\ell_p-L_e\) and \(x_2=\ell_p+W+L_h\) (slides 139–144):
\[
I_{ph}=\frac{e\eta_iTP_o}{h\nu}\left[e^{-\alpha x_1}-e^{-\alpha x_2}\right],
\qquad \text{pin with thin p}^+:\ I_{ph}\approx\frac{e\eta_iTP_o}{h\nu}\left[1-e^{-\alpha W}\right].
\]
At short λ (large α) light is absorbed in the p⁺ layer and near the surface, where carriers recombine; at long λ (small α) it passes through the collecting region. The responsivity peaks in between. Because \(\eta_e=\mathcal Rhc/e\lambda\), the QE is maximum where \(d(\mathcal R/\lambda)/d\lambda=0\), i.e. where \(d\mathcal R/d\lambda=\mathcal R/\lambda\): the tangent to the \(\mathcal R(\lambda)\) curve passes through the origin (slide 26). That point is not the peak of \(\mathcal R\).

title: 5  The pin photodiode
text:
5.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 29–30 (structure, field and capacitance of the pin photodiode), 31 (drift velocity in Si), 32 (diffusion of carriers generated in the p⁺ layer), 37–40 (worked examples: transit time, diffusion time) and 41–43 (steady-state photocurrent).
A pn junction has a narrow depletion region whose width depends on the bias (Ch. 3), so most light is absorbed in the neutral regions and collected slowly by diffusion. The pin photodiode inserts an intrinsic (lightly doped) layer of width \(W\) between p⁺ and n⁺ (slide 29). The depletion region is the whole i-layer, nearly independent of the bias, with a uniform field (slide 30):
\[
E=E_o+\frac{V_r}{W}\approx\frac{V_r}{W},\qquad C_\text{dep}=\frac{\varepsilon_o\varepsilon_rA}{W},\qquad
t_\text{drift}=\frac{W}{v_d}.
\]
The drift velocity saturates at high field, about \(10^5\) m/s for electrons in Si above \(\sim3\times10^6\) V/m (slide 31), so the transit time cannot be reduced indefinitely by raising \(V_r\). Carriers generated in the p⁺ layer outside the field must diffuse to the i-layer; in a time \(t\) they diffuse on average (slide 32)
\[
\ell=\sqrt{2D_et}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad t_\text{diff}=\frac{\ell^2}{2D_e},
\]
which is much slower than drift and produces the slow diffusion tail of the pulse response (Chapter 9).
The pin therefore embodies the central trade-off of photodetection: a wide \(W\) absorbs more light (high \(\mathcal R\), Chapter 4) and has a small capacitance (small \(RC\)), but a long transit time. A narrow \(W\) is fast in transit but absorbs little and has a large capacitance. For a given load there is an optimum width.

title: 6  Avalanche photodiodes
text:
6.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 44–48 (structure of the reach-through APD, impact ionisation, multiplication, temperature dependence, guard ring), 49 (comparison of photodiodes), 50–51 (ionisation coefficients, Chynoweth’s law, multiplication for electrons only and for both carriers), 52–55 (SAM and SAGM InGaAs/InP APDs, reach-through characteristics), 56–59 (worked examples) and 60 (superlattice APD).
In an APD a primary photocarrier is accelerated by a field of several 10⁵ V/cm until it gains enough kinetic energy (more than about \(\frac32E_g\)) to excite a valence electron across the gap: impact ionisation (slide 45). Each ionisation creates a new pair, which is itself accelerated: an avalanche. The multiplication is (slide 46)
\[
M=\frac{I_{ph}}{I_{pho}},\qquad \mathcal R_{APD}=M\mathcal R_{M=1},\qquad
M\approx\frac{1}{1-(V_r/V_{br})^m}\ \text{(empirical, } m\approx3\text{–}6).
\]
The ionisation coefficient α is the number of ionisations per unit distance. It rises steeply with the field (Chynoweth’s law, slide 50), and electrons and holes have different coefficients, with the ratio \(k\):
\[
\alpha_e=A\exp(-B/E),\qquad k=\frac{\alpha_h}{\alpha_e}.
\]
For electrons injected into a uniform avalanche region of width \(w\) (slide 51):
\[
M_e=\exp(\alpha_ew)\ \ (\text{electrons only, }k=0),\qquad
M=\frac{1-k}{\exp[-(1-k)\alpha_ew]-k}\ \ (\text{both carriers}).
\]
With \(k=0\) the gain grows smoothly with the field. With \(k>0\) the holes created by the electrons travel backwards and ionise too: a feedback loop. When \(\exp[-(1-k)\alpha_ew]=k\) the denominator vanishes and the current runs away: avalanche breakdown. A good APD material has \(k\ll1\) (Si: \(k\approx0.02\)–\(0.1\)) and the avalanche must be started by the carrier with the larger coefficient. The same \(k\) also sets the noise (Chapter 11).
Practical structures separate the two jobs. The Si reach-through APD (\(n^+p\pi p^+\), slide 44) absorbs in a wide, low-field π region and multiplies in a thin, high-field \(pn^+\) region. The InGaAs/InP SAM APD (slides 52–54) absorbs in InGaAs (1.55 µm) and multiplies in InP, where the field is high but the gap wide enough to avoid tunnelling; a graded InGaAsP layer (SAGM) removes the valence-band step \(\Delta E_v\) that would trap the holes at the heterointerface (slide 53).

TipGoing further






Non-uniform fields. Real avalanche regions have a triangular or trapezoidal field. Use dl.apd_gain_profile(x, αe(x), αh(x)), which integrates McIntyre’s general expression, for a p⁺n junction with a linear field and compare with a uniform field of the same peak value. Which carries more gain, the peak or the average?
Dead space. A carrier must travel a minimum distance \(d=E_i/eE\) before it can ionise again. In thin (≲ 100 nm) multiplication layers this makes the ionisation positions less random, which lowers the excess noise below McIntyre’s prediction: the basis of thin InAlAs and AlInAsSb APDs.
Geiger mode and SPADs. Biased above breakdown, an APD stays quiescent until a single carrier triggers a self-sustaining avalanche, which a quenching resistor stops: a single-photon avalanche diode. Count the photons, not the current. Photon-detection efficiency, dark-count rate, dead time and after-pulsing replace QE, dark current and bandwidth. SPAD arrays are the receivers of automotive lidar and of quantum-key-distribution links.

title: 7  Schottky, MSM and phototransistors
text:
7.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 61–65 (Schottky junction, barrier, dark current, Schottky photodiodes and their characteristics), 66–67 (metal–semiconductor–metal detectors with interdigitated electrodes) and 68 (phototransistor).
Schottky photodiode. A metal with a work function \(\Phi_m\) larger than that of an n-type semiconductor (electron affinity \(\chi\)) forms a rectifying contact: electrons flow from the semiconductor into the metal until the Fermi levels align, leaving a depletion region in the semiconductor and a barrier (slide 62)
\[
\Phi_B=\Phi_m-\chi
\]
for electrons in the metal. In reverse bias the dark current is the thermionic emission of electrons from the metal over this barrier (slide 63):
\[
J_\text{dark}\approx A^*T^2\exp\!\left(-\frac{\Phi_B}{k_BT}\right),\qquad A^*=\frac{4\pi em^*k_B^2}{h^3}\approx1.2\times10^6\frac{m^*}{m_e}\ \text{A m}^{-2}\text{K}^{-2}.
\]
Light with \(h\nu>E_g\) passes through a thin, semitransparent metal and is absorbed in the depletion region, right at the surface (slide 64). There is no neutral p⁺ “dead layer” as in a pn diode, so Schottky photodiodes have an excellent UV and blue response and are fast: only drift in the field, no minority-carrier diffusion (table of slide 65: GaAsP, GaP, AlGaN for UV; GaAs with \(\tau_r<30\) ps).
MSM detector. Two Schottky contacts back to back on the same surface, usually as interdigitated fingers (slides 66–67). Under bias the region between the fingers is fully depleted. Both the transit length (the finger gap \(s\)) and the capacitance (planar electrodes, no parallel-plate junction) are small, so MSM detectors reach tens of GHz. The price: the fingers shadow part of the area (fill factor \(s/(s+w_f)\)), and the field is weak deep below the surface.
Phototransistor. A bipolar transistor whose base–collector junction is the photodiode (slide 68). The photogenerated holes swept into the base act as base current, and transistor action multiplies the collector current:
\[
I_{ph}\approx\beta I_{pho}.
\]
The gain is free, but the base must be charged through the emitter resistance \(r_e=k_BT/eI_C\): the bandwidth \(f_{3dB}\approx1/(2\pi\beta r_eC)=I_{pho}/(2\pi(k_BT/e)C)\) is proportional to the primary photocurrent. Bright light makes it fast, dim light makes it slow.

title: 8  Photoconductive detectors
text:
8.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 69–71 (photoconductive detectors, ohmic contacts and gain), 72 (photoconductivity and photocurrent density), 73–74 (photoconductive gain and transit times) and 146–148 (PbS, PbSe and InSb photoconductors, chopper and lock-in detection).
A photoconductor is just a slab of semiconductor of length \(\ell\), width \(w\) and thickness \(d\) with two ohmic contacts (slide 70). Light creates excess carriers \(\Delta n=\Delta p\) that raise the conductivity. Under a steady photon flux the generation rate per unit volume is \(g_{ph}=\eta_iI\lambda/(hcd)\) for an intensity \(I\) absorbed in the thickness \(d\), and the excess density settles at \(\Delta n=g_{ph}\tau\), with τ the recombination lifetime (slide 72):
\[
\Delta\sigma=e\Delta n(\mu_e+\mu_h)=\frac{e\eta_iI\lambda\tau(\mu_e+\mu_h)}{hcd},\qquad J_{ph}=\Delta\sigma\frac{V}{\ell}=\Delta\sigma E .
\]
The photoconductive gain compares the rate of electrons flowing in the external circuit with the rate of pair generation (slides 73–74):
\[
G=\frac{\tau(\mu_e+\mu_h)E}{\ell}=\frac{\tau}{t_e}+\frac{\tau}{t_h}=\frac{\tau}{t_e}\left(1+\frac{\mu_h}{\mu_e}\right),\qquad
t_e=\frac{\ell}{\mu_eE},\ t_h=\frac{\ell}{\mu_hE}.
\]
\(G\) can be much larger than 1. The reason is charge neutrality with ohmic contacts (slide 71): while a slow hole (or a hole trapped at a defect) is still in the slab, every electron that leaves at the anode is replaced by a new one injected at the cathode. One absorbed photon therefore lets \(\tau/t_e\) electrons circulate. The catch is speed: the photocurrent rises and decays with the lifetime τ, so the bandwidth is about \(1/2\pi\tau\) and
\[
G\times B\approx\frac{\tau}{t_e}\cdot\frac{1}{2\pi\tau}=\frac{1}{2\pi t_e}=\frac{\mu_eV}{2\pi\ell^2}
\]
is independent of τ: gain is bought with bandwidth. Photoconductors (PbS, PbSe, InSb, HgCdTe, CdS light-dependent resistors) are used where a simple, sensitive, slow detector is enough: radiation thermometers, flame monitors, gas analysers, spectrometers in the 1–6 µm range (slides 69, 146).

title: 9  Photodiode circuits and speed
text:
9.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 75–76 (reverse-biased photodiode with a load resistor, load line, operating point), 77 (transimpedance amplifier), 78–80 (equivalent circuit, cut-off frequency), 81 (a commercial APD photoreceiver), 82–85 (pulsed excitation, rise and fall times, RC-limited and drift/diffusion-limited responses).
Load line. A photodiode reverse biased by \(V_r\) through a load \(R_L\) (slide 75) must satisfy both its own I–V curve and Kirchhoff’s law for the loop (slide 76):
\[
I=-\frac{V+V_r}{R_L}\quad\text{(load line)},\qquad I=I_o\left[e^{eV/\eta k_BT}-1\right]-I_{ph}\quad\text{(photodiode)}.
\]
The operating point P is their intersection. As long as P stays in the reverse-bias region, \(I\approx-I_{ph}\) and the output voltage \(|I|R_L\) is linear in the power. When \(I_{ph}R_L\) approaches \(V_r\), the diode is pushed towards forward bias and the response saturates.
Transimpedance amplifier (TIA). An op-amp with a feedback resistor \(R_F\) holds the photodiode at virtual ground (or at \(-V_r\)) and converts the current into \(V_\text{out}=-I_{ph}R_F\) (slide 77). The diode never sees a voltage swing, so the response is linear, and the bandwidth is no longer \(1/2\pi R_FC_d\) (see the panel).
Equivalent circuit and bandwidth. A real photodiode is a current source \(I_{ph}\) in parallel with the ideal diode, the depletion plus package capacitance \(C_t\) and a shunt resistance \(R_p\), followed by a series resistance \(R_s\) (slides 78–79). For signals faster than the drift and diffusion times are negligible, the bandwidth is set by the \(RC\) time constant (slide 80):
\[
f_c=\frac{1}{2\pi R_\text{eq}C_t}\approx\frac{1}{2\pi(R_s+R_L)C_t}\approx\frac{1}{2\pi R_LC_t},\qquad
R_\text{eq}=(R_s+R_L)\parallel R_p .
\]
Rise and fall times. For a step of light, an RC circuit charges as \(1-e^{-t/\tau}\) with \(\tau=(R_s+R_L)C_t\). The 10–90 % rise time and the 90–10 % fall time are (slides 83–84)
\[
\tau_r=\tau_F=2.2\,\tau,\qquad f_c=\frac{1}{2\pi\tau}=\frac{0.35}{\tau_r}=\frac{350\ \text{MHz}}{\tau_r\ [\text{ns}]}.
\]
When the \(RC\) constant is small, the pulse shows the device physics instead (slide 85): a fast drift component from carriers generated in the depletion region and a slow diffusion tail from carriers generated in the neutral regions (Chapter 5).

title: 10  Noise, SNR, NEP and detectivity
text:
10.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 86–91 (noise current, shot noise, Poisson statistics, dark-current and quantum noise), 92–93 (thermal noise of the load), 94 (SNR), 95–98 (NEP, detectivity, noise data of commercial detectors, NEP versus dark current) and 101–105 (worked examples: ideal photodetector, NEP of a Si pin, SNR of a receiver).
Under constant illumination the photocurrent is not constant: it fluctuates around its mean (slide 86). The noise is quantified by the RMS of the fluctuations, \(i_n=\sqrt{\overline{(i-\bar\imath)^2}}\), within the measurement bandwidth \(B\).
Shot noise. Electrons cross the junction one by one, at random times: the number \(N\) counted in a time \(T\) follows Poisson statistics, \(\sigma_N^2=\bar N\) (slide 87). For a current \(I=e\bar N/T\) measured in a bandwidth \(B=1/2T\), this gives (slides 89–90)
\[
i_{n}^2=2eIB,\qquad i_n=\left[2e(I_d+I_{ph})B\right]^{1/2}.
\]
The dark current and the photocurrent both have shot noise. The photocurrent part is called quantum noise: it reflects the random arrival of photons and cannot be removed.
Thermal (Johnson) noise. The carriers in the load resistor have random thermal velocities (slide 88). The available noise power is \(4k_BTB\), so the noise current of \(R_L\) is (slide 92)
\[
i_\text{th}=\left[\frac{4k_BTB}{R_L}\right]^{1/2}.
\]
Signal-to-noise ratio. Independent noise sources add in power (mean squares), never in amplitude (slides 93–94):
\[
\text{SNR}=\frac{\text{signal power}}{\text{noise power}}=\frac{I_{ph}^2}{2e(I_d+I_{ph})B+4k_BTB/R_L} .
\]
Noise equivalent power and detectivity. The NEP is the optical power that gives SNR = 1 in a 1 Hz bandwidth (slide 95); the detectivity is its inverse, and the specific detectivity normalises by the square root of the area, because for many detectors the noise power scales with area (slide 96):
\[
\text{NEP}=\frac{P_1}{B^{1/2}}=\frac{1}{\mathcal R}\left[2e(I_d+I_{ph})\right]^{1/2}\ [\text{W Hz}^{-1/2}],\qquad
D^*=\frac{A^{1/2}}{\text{NEP}}\ [\text{cm Hz}^{1/2}\text{W}^{-1}=\text{Jones}].
\]
For an ideal detector (\(\eta=1\), \(I_d=0\), no thermal noise) the minimum power for SNR = 1 is (slide 101)
\[
P_1=\frac{2hcB}{\eta\lambda}.
\]

WarningTwo subtleties hidden in slides 95 and 102






NEP of an ideal detector is not a constant. For an ideal detector \(P_1=2hcB/\lambda\) grows linearly with \(B\), so \(\text{NEP}=P_1/\sqrt B\) grows as \(\sqrt B\). The statement “NEP = \(2hc/\lambda\)” of slide 102 is only true numerically at \(B=1\) Hz. The NEP is bandwidth-independent only when the noise does not depend on the signal (dark current, thermal noise): then \(P_1\propto\sqrt B\).
The NEP formula contains \(I_{ph}\). In \(\text{NEP}=[2e(I_d+I_{ph})]^{1/2}/\mathcal R\) the photocurrent is that of the power \(P_1\) being sought; the usual datasheet value assumes \(I_{ph}\ll I_d\). It also ignores the amplifier and load, which dominate most real receivers.










TipGoing further






Where does \(2eIB\) come from? A train of random δ-pulses of charge \(e\) at rate \(r\) has a flat two-sided power spectral density \(e^2r=eI\) (Campbell’s theorem); the one-sided density is \(2eI\). Verify it numerically: generate Poisson arrivals, compute the periodogram with numpy.fft, and compare with \(2eI\).
The noise of a photon stream depends on the source. Laser light far above threshold is Poissonian (coherent state); thermal (chaotic) light within one mode has excess noise \(\sigma_N^2=\bar N+\bar N^2\); “squeezed” light can be quieter than Poisson. Shot noise is therefore a property of the light and of the detection.
Background-limited infrared photodetectors (BLIP). In the 3–12 µm range the detector sees the 300 K world (Planck, Ch. 4): the shot noise of the background photocurrent sets \(D^*_\text{BLIP}=\frac{\lambda}{hc}\sqrt{\frac{\eta}{2\Phi_B}}\). Compute \(\Phi_B\) for a detector with a 60° field of view and a 5 µm cut-off, and the resulting \(D^*\). Why do thermal cameras use cold shields?
1/f noise dominates at low frequencies in photoconductors and in dark currents; chopping and lock-in detection

shift the measurement above the 1/f corner.

title: 11  Noise in avalanche photodiodes
text:
11.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 99–100 (multiplied shot noise, excess avalanche noise factor F ≈ Mˣ) and 106–107 (worked example: noise in an InGaAs APD).
An APD multiplies the primary photocurrent and dark current by \(M\). If every primary carrier produced exactly \(M\) secondaries, the shot noise would be multiplied too, \(i_n=M[2e(I_{do}+I_{pho})B]^{1/2}\), and the SNR would be unchanged (slide 99). But impact ionisation is random: some carriers travel far before ionising, others ionise at once (slide 100). The gain itself fluctuates, and the noise is larger by the excess noise factor \(F=\langle M^2\rangle/\langle M\rangle^2\):
\[
i_{n\text{-APD}}=\left[2e(I_{do}+I_{pho})M^2FB\right]^{1/2},\qquad F\approx M^x .
\]
\(x\approx0.3\)–\(0.5\) for Si, \(0.7\)–\(1\) for Ge and InGaAs/InP (slide 100). McIntyre’s theory for a uniform avalanche region, with the avalanche started by the carrier of larger coefficient and \(k\) the ratio of the smaller to the larger coefficient, gives
\[
F=kM+(1-k)\left(2-\frac1M\right),
\]
so \(F\to2\) at high gain when \(k=0\), and \(F\approx M\) when \(k=1\). The SNR of an APD receiver with a load \(R_L\) is
\[
\text{SNR}=\frac{M^2I_{pho}^2}{2e(I_{do}+I_{pho})M^2FB+4k_BTB/R_L}.
\]
Gain helps against the thermal noise of the load and amplifier, which is not multiplied, but it adds excess noise to the shot noise. There is therefore an optimum gain: above it, \(M^2F\) grows faster than \(M^2\) and the SNR falls.

Optimum gain analytically. With \(F=M^x\) and dark current neglected, maximise the SNR: \(M_\text{opt}^{2+x}=\frac{4k_BT/R_L}{xe(I_{pho}+I_{do})}\). Check it against the panel. Why does the optimum decrease when the signal increases?
Gain–bandwidth product. With \(k>0\) the avalanche takes several round trips of electrons and holes to build up; at high gain the bandwidth falls as \(f_{3dB}\approx1/(2\pi M k\tau_{av})\), a constant gain–bandwidth product (100–300 GHz for InGaAs/InAlAs APDs). Small \(k\) is good for noise and speed.
Electron-APDs. HgCdTe and InAs APDs have \(k\approx0\) and \(F\approx1\)–\(1.3\) up to \(M=100\): the avalanche is deterministic, almost a noiseless amplifier. They are used for single-photon-sensitive infrared imaging.
Compare with an optical preamplifier (Ch. 4): an EDFA before a pin has a noise figure of about 3 dB, i.e. an effective “\(F\)” of 2 with \(M=G\approx1000\) and THz of optical bandwidth (Chapter 14).

title: 12  Image sensors: CCD and CMOS
text:
12.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
Slides 108–111 (CCD and CMOS image sensors, image sensing with a pixel array, colour imaging with a Bayer filter or three CCDs), 112 (active-matrix readout), 113 (CMOS pixel, microlenses and colour filters), 114–117 (the CCD element and three-phase charge transfer) and 118–120 (full-frame, frame-transfer and interline-transfer architectures).
An image sensor is an array of photosensitive pixels, each integrating the photogenerated charge during the exposure time (slide 110). The signal of a pixel, in electrons, is
\[
S=\eta\,\Phi_{ph}\,A_\text{pix}\,t_\text{exp}\le N_\text{FW},
\]
with \(\eta\) the QE (including the fill factor and the microlens), \(\Phi_{ph}\) the photon flux density, and \(N_\text{FW}\) the full-well capacity. The noise combines the photon shot noise of the signal, the shot noise of the dark charge \(D\) and the read noise \(\sigma_r\) of the output amplifier (in electrons rms):
\[
\text{SNR}=\frac{S}{\sqrt{S+D+\sigma_r^2}},\qquad \text{dynamic range}=\frac{N_\text{FW}}{\sigma_r}.
\]
CCD. Each pixel is a MOS capacitor: a positive gate voltage on p-type Si creates a depletion region, a potential well that stores the photogenerated electrons (slide 115). By clocking three interleaved gate phases the wells move and the packets are shifted, without mixing, one gate at a time (slides 116–117): three clock steps move a packet by one pixel. The packets are shifted row by row into a serial register and then pixel by pixel to a single, very low-noise output amplifier (slide 118). A packet that is transferred \(N\) times with a charge-transfer efficiency CTE keeps a fraction \(\text{CTE}^N\). Frame-transfer and interline architectures (slides 119–120) add a light-shielded storage area so the next exposure can start while the previous frame is read.
CMOS. Each pixel has its own photodiode and transistors (reset, source follower, row select: the 3T pixel of slide 113) and is addressed like a memory (row and column decoders, active matrix of slide 112). There is no charge transfer across the chip, the readout is fast and parallel, and the logic, ADCs and image processing are integrated on the same chip; the price was historically a higher read noise and fixed-pattern noise, now largely overcome. Colour is obtained with a Bayer mosaic of red, green and blue filters (twice as many green as red or blue pixels, like the eye’s sensitivity) or, in professional cameras, with three sensors behind a trichroic prism (slide 111).

Slides 121–124 (pn junction solar cell, I–V characteristics under illumination, short-circuit current and open-circuit voltage), 125–126 (load line and fill factor), 127–129 (equivalent circuit, series and shunt resistance), 130–132 (efficiencies, textured surfaces, tandem cells) and 133–137 (worked examples).
A solar cell is a large-area pn junction operated in the fourth quadrant of the I–V plane (slide 122): it generates a current while the voltage across it is positive, so it delivers power \(P=-IV\) to a load. With the convention of slide 123,
\[
I=-I_{ph}+I_o\left[\exp\!\left(\frac{eV}{\eta k_BT}\right)-1\right],\qquad I_{ph}=K\,I_\text{light},
\]
where \(K\) is a device constant and \(I_\text{light}\) the light intensity (slide 124). Two limits characterise the cell:
\[
I_{sc}=-I_{ph},\qquad V_{oc}=\frac{\eta k_BT}{e}\ln\!\left(\frac{I_{ph}}{I_o}+1\right).
\]
With a load \(R\) the operating point is the intersection of the cell curve with the load line \(I=-V/R\) (slide 125). The power is the area of the rectangle \(|IV|\); it is maximum at the maximum power point \((V_m,I_m)\), and the fill factor measures how “square” the curve is (slide 126):
\[
\text{FF}=\frac{I_mV_m}{I_{sc}V_{oc}},\qquad \text{efficiency}=\frac{I_mV_m}{P_\text{in}}=\frac{\text{FF}\,I_{sc}V_{oc}}{I_\text{light}A}.
\]
Real cells have a series resistance \(R_s\) (finger electrodes, thin emitter, contacts) and a shunt resistance \(R_p\) (leakage at edges and defects) (slides 127–128):
\[
I=-I_{ph}+I_o\left[\exp\!\left(\frac{e(V-IR_s)}{\eta k_BT}\right)-1\right]+\frac{V-IR_s}{R_p}.
\]
\(R_s\) tilts the curve near \(V_{oc}\) and reduces the FF and eventually \(I_{sc}\) (slide 129); a small \(R_p\) tilts it near \(I_{sc}\).

14.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
This chapter is not in the slides. It connects the noise analysis of Chapter 10 and Chapter 11 with the bit-error rate of Ch. 2 and the optical amplifiers of Ch. 4, and answers the question every link designer asks: how many photons does one bit need?
A digital receiver decides, bit by bit, whether a “1” or a “0” was sent by comparing the photocurrent with a threshold. With on–off keying (OOK) the “1” gives a mean current \(I_1\) with noise \(\sigma_1\) and the “0” gives \(I_0\) with noise \(\sigma_0\). For Gaussian noise and the optimum threshold, the bit-error rate depends only on the Q factor (Ch. 2):
\[
Q=\frac{I_1-I_0}{\sigma_1+\sigma_0},\qquad \text{BER}=\frac12\operatorname{erfc}\!\left(\frac{Q}{\sqrt2}\right),\qquad
\text{BER}=10^{-9}\Leftrightarrow Q=6,\quad 10^{-12}\Leftrightarrow Q=7.03 .
\]
The sensitivity is the average optical power \(\bar P=(P_1+P_0)/2\) that gives the target BER. With \(P_0=0\), a photodiode of responsivity \(\mathcal R\) and an electrical bandwidth \(B_e\approx R_b/2\) for a bit rate \(R_b\):

pin, thermal-noise limited (\(\sigma_0=\sigma_1=\sigma_T\), the noise of the load or TIA): \(\bar P=Q\sigma_T/\mathcal R\). It grows as \(\sqrt{B_e}\) and is independent of the photon energy.
pin, shot-noise limited (ideal amplifier): \(\bar P=Q^2eB_e/\mathcal R\), i.e. \(Q^2/2\approx18\) photons per bit for \(\eta=1\) at BER \(10^{-9}\) (with \(B_e=R_b/2\)).
APD: the signal is multiplied by \(M\), the thermal noise is not, and the shot noise gets the excess factor \(F\); there is an optimum \(M\) (Chapter 11).
Optically preamplified (EDFA + pin, Ch. 4): the amplifier gain \(G\) lifts the signal far above the thermal noise; the noise is now the beat between the signal and the amplified spontaneous emission, \(\sigma^2_{s\text{-}sp}=4\mathcal R^2GP_1S_{sp}B_e\), with \(S_{sp}=n_{sp}(G-1)h\nu\), plus the ASE–ASE beat in the optical bandwidth \(B_o\).
Quantum limit: an ideal photon counter makes an error only when a “1” produces no photoelectron at all, with probability \(e^{-N_1}\). \(\text{BER}=\frac12e^{-N_1}\) gives \(N_1=20\) photons in a “1”, i.e. 10 photons per bit on average at BER \(10^{-9}\).

14.4 Why it matters: the link budget
Ch. 2 computed the attenuation of a fiber; Ch. 4 the launch power of a laser. The receiver sensitivity closes the budget: \(P_\text{launch}-\alpha L-\text{penalties}\ge\bar P_\text{sens}\). With 0 dBm launched, 0.2 dB/km and 3 dB of margin, the 10 Gb/s pin receiver above reaches about 100 km, the APD about 150 km, and the preamplified receiver about 180 km (before dispersion, Ch. 2, becomes the limit). Long-haul links put amplifiers every 80 km instead, and their accumulated ASE, not the receiver, sets the OSNR (Ch. 4).






TipGoing further






Coherent detection. Mixing the signal with a strong local oscillator \(P_{LO}\) on the photodiode gives a beat current \(2\mathcal R\sqrt{P_sP_{LO}}\) that can be made far larger than the thermal noise; the receiver becomes shot-noise limited by the LO. Show that the SNR then approaches \(\eta P_s/(h\nu B)\) and that heterodyne PSK needs about 18 photons per bit for BER \(10^{-9}\). Coherent receivers with balanced photodiodes and DSP carry 400–800 Gb/s per wavelength today.
Photon counting at the quantum limit. Deep-space optical links (NASA’s DSOC on Psyche, 2023) use superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors and pulse-position modulation to reach ~1 photon per bit or less. Why can PPM beat the 10 photons/bit of OOK?
Non-Gaussian statistics. The APD gain and the ASE beat noise are not Gaussian; the Gaussian Q approximation overestimates the required power for APDs (McIntyre distribution) by about 1 dB.
Extinction ratio penalty. If the “0” carries a power \(P_0=rP_1\) (laser biased above threshold, Ch. 4), the thermal-limited sensitivity degrades by \((1+r)/(1-r)\). Compute the penalty for \(r=0.1\).

title: 15  Going further: the Shockley–Queisser limit
text:
15.1 Key relations
Run this chapter’s code in Google Colab (no installation).
This chapter is not in the slides. Slide 130 lists record efficiencies of 25–32 %; here we ask why no single-junction cell can do much better, using the black-body radiation and detailed balance of Ch. 4.
Treat the Sun as a black body at \(T_s\approx5800\) K seen under a small solid angle, and the cell as a semiconductor of band gap \(E_g\) at \(T_c=300\) K. Shockley and Queisser (1961) made four assumptions: every photon with \(h\nu\ge E_g\) is absorbed and gives exactly one electron–hole pair; photons below \(E_g\) are lost; the carriers relax to the band edges (the excess energy is lost as heat); and the only recombination is radiative, as required by detailed balance. The photon flux of a black body per unit photon energy, emitted into a hemisphere, is
\[
\phi_{bb}(E,T)=\frac{2\pi}{h^3c^2}\frac{E^2}{e^{E/k_BT}-1}.
\]
The Sun is diluted by the factor \(f=(R_\odot/d_\text{Earth})^2\approx2.16\times10^{-5}\) (the solid angle of the solar disc over π), so
\[
J_{sc}=ef\int_{E_g}^\infty\phi_{bb}(E,T_s)\,dE,\qquad J_0=e\int_{E_g}^\infty\phi_{bb}(E,T_c)\,dE .
\]
In the dark the cell must emit as many photons as it absorbs from its 300 K surroundings: that radiative emission is the dark current \(J_0\), and under bias it grows as \(e^{eV/k_BT_c}\). The I–V curve is that of an ideal diode, \(J=J_{sc}-J_0(e^{eV/k_BT_c}-1)\), and the efficiency is the maximum of \(JV\) divided by the incident power \(f\sigma T_s^4\approx1360\) W/m². A small gap absorbs many photons but gives a low voltage; a large gap gives a high voltage but wastes most photons. The optimum, about 30.5 % at \(E_g\approx1.3\) eV for black-body sunlight (33.7 % for the real AM1.5 spectrum at 1.34 eV), is the Shockley–Queisser limit.

For Si the black-body spectrum gives \(J_{sc}\approx53\) mA/cm²; the real AM1.5 spectrum, depleted in the infrared by water and CO₂ absorption, gives 43.8 mA/cm², very close to the 42.7 mA/cm² of the PERL record cell: crystalline Si collects almost every photon. Its voltage, 0.707 V instead of the radiative-limit 0.85–0.88 V, is where the remaining gap lies: Auger and surface recombination (Ch. 3) replace the purely radiative \(J_0\) of the ideal cell.

text:
15.4 Two junctions (slide 132)


Show the Python
def cell_eff(Eg_lo, Eg_hi, Ts=5778.0, Tc=300.0):
    f = (6.957e8/1.496e11)**2
    E = np.linspace(Eg_lo, Eg_hi, 1500)
    Jsc = dl.qe*f*np.trapezoid(dl._photon_flux_bb(E, Ts), E)
    Ec = np.linspace(Eg_lo, Eg_lo + 40*dl.kT(Tc), 1500)
    J0 = dl.qe*np.trapezoid(dl._photon_flux_bb(Ec, Tc), Ec)
    V = np.linspace(0, dl.kT(Tc)*np.log(Jsc/J0 + 1), 800)
    return (V*(Jsc - J0*np.expm1(V/dl.kT(Tc)))).max()/(f*dl.sigma_SB*Ts**4)
g1 = np.linspace(1.3, 2.4, 34); g2 = np.linspace(0.6, 1.5, 28)
Z = np.array([[cell_eff(a, 6.0) + cell_eff(b, a) if a > b else np.nan for a in g1] for b in g2])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4.4))
cs = ax.contourf(g1, g2, 100*Z, levels=np.arange(28, 47, 1), cmap="viridis"); fig.colorbar(cs, label="efficiency (%)")
i, j = np.unravel_index(np.nanargmax(Z), Z.shape); ax.plot(g1[j], g2[i], "w*", ms=12)
ax.plot(1.95, 1.42, "rx", ms=10, mew=2)
ax.set(xlabel="top-cell gap E_g1 (eV)", ylabel="bottom-cell gap E_g2 (eV)", title=f"max {100*np.nanmax(Z):.1f} % at ({g1[j]:.2f}, {g2[i]:.2f}) eV"); plt.show()








Figure 15.1: Detailed-balance efficiency of a four-terminal (independently connected) tandem: the top cell absorbs hν > E_g1, the bottom cell E_g2 < hν < E_g1. The optimum near (1.8, 0.93) eV gives about 42 %. The GaInP/GaAs pair of slide 132 (1.95/1.42 eV, ×) is well off the peak: its bottom gap is too wide and wastes the infrared, which is why the triple-junction cell adds a Ge (0.66 eV) cell underneath.











TipGoing further






Infinite junctions. With an infinite stack of cells, each converting a narrow slice of the spectrum, the limit rises to 68 % (one sun) and 86 % (full concentration). Extend the tandem code to \(N\) cells with equal photon currents.
Photon recycling and external luminescence. A real cell has non-radiative recombination: \(V_{oc}=V_{oc}^{SQ}+\frac{k_BT}{e}\ln\eta_\text{ext}\), where \(\eta_\text{ext}\) is the external luminescence efficiency. “A great solar cell must be a great LED” (Miller, Yablonovitch, 2012): connect this with the LED efficiency of Ch. 3. GaAs record cells have \(\eta_\text{ext}\approx30\) %.
Hot-carrier cells and singlet fission try to recover the thermalisation loss; intermediate-band cells and up-conversion try to use sub-gap photons. What do they need to beat 31 %?
Thermodynamic limit. Even an ideal converter is limited by Carnot (1 − 300/5800 = 95 %) and, more strictly, by the Landsberg limit (93 %). Where does the remaining loss of the SQ cell come from in thermodynamic terms (entropy of the absorbed photons, étendue expansion from the solar disc to the hemisphere)?










NoteComplements

O. D. Miller, E. Yablonovitch, S. R. Kurtz, “Strong internal and external luminescence as solar cells approach the Shockley–Queisser limit”, IEEE J. Photovolt. 2, 303 (2012).
S. Rühle, “Tabulated values of the Shockley–Queisser limit for single junction solar cells”, Sol. Energy 130, 139 (2016) (AM1.5 values).

15.5 Try it yourself

Show that \(J_0\) for Si at 300 K is of order \(10^{-12}\) A/m² in the radiative limit, and compare with the \(10^{-9}\)–\(10^{-8}\) A/m² of real Si cells. How many millivolts of \(V_{oc}\) does that cost?

16.4 Improvements to the course

One trade-off per device. Each detector of the chapter trades something for something: thickness for speed (pin), gain for noise (APD), gain for bandwidth (photoconductor, phototransistor), fill factor for speed (MSM), voltage for current (solar cell band gap). Framing the chapter this way, with the live panels of Chapter 5, Chapter 11 and Chapter 8, makes it coherent.
“Predict, then compute.” “Does doubling the light double V_oc?”, “Does raising V_r make a pin faster?”, “Does a higher APD gain always improve the SNR?”, “Is a detector with R = 100 A/W better than one with R = 0.5 A/W?”
Close the link budget. The receiver chapter (Chapter 14) ties Ch. 2 (BER, attenuation, dispersion), Ch. 4 (EDFA noise) and Ch. 5 (photodiode noise) into a single calculation: a good capstone exercise.
Lab connection. A Si photodiode, a few LEDs of different colours, a load resistor box, an oscilloscope and a small solar panel cover responsivity, the load line, the RC response and the fill factor in one afternoon.
Modern content. Possible updates: Ge-on-Si waveguide photodiodes for silicon photonics, SPAD arrays for lidar, SNSPDs, backside-illuminated stacked CMOS sensors, perovskite and perovskite/Si tandem solar cells, coherent receivers.

16.5 Notes for the instructor: checks on the slides
While recomputing the examples, everything matched the slides (QE and responsivity examples, pin transit and diffusion times, steady-state photocurrent with and without AR coating, Table 5.7, APD responsivities, Chynoweth example, ideal-detector and NEP examples, receiver SNR, APD noise example, solar-cell load line, \(V_{oc}\) versus intensity, efficiency table), except these points:

Slide numbering: the companion uses the 152 slides of chapter5_ Photodetectors.ppt.
Slide 20: the column header “\(\lambda_g\) (eV)” should read “\(\lambda_g\) (µm)” (Chapter 3).
Slide 16: the In₀.₅₃Ga₀.₄₇As curve gives about \(2\times10^5\) m⁻¹ at 1.55 µm, three times below literature values (\(\approx7\times10^5\) m⁻¹); the companion uses the literature values for InGaAs.
Slide 40: “at this field the drift velocity saturates at \(10^5\) m s⁻¹”: at \(3\times10^6\) V/m the Caughey–Thomas model gives \(0.89\times10^5\) m/s (0.22 ns instead of 0.2 ns); the conclusion is unchanged (Chapter 5).
Slide 49: the dark current of the GaP pin is printed “1 nm” (1 nA); the footnote letters are shuffled (“ᶜFGAP71” should be “ᵃ”).
Slide 56: “\(R=MR=(12)/(0.75)\)” should be \((12)(0.75)=9.0\) A/W (Chapter 6).
Slide 59 (Table 5.3): with unrounded coefficients \(M=58.7\) at \(4.30\times10^5\) V/cm and 644 at \(4.38\times10^5\) V/cm (slide: 57.2 and 647). The difference comes from rounding \(k\) to three digits and illustrates how sensitive \(M\) is near breakdown.
Slide 97: the GaP Schottky NEP (\(5.4\times10^{-15}\) W Hz⁻¹ᐟ²) is three times lower than the shot-noise value for the quoted \(I_d=10\) pA; the other entries agree with \(\sqrt{2eI_d}/\mathcal R\) within 20 % (Chapter 10).
Slide 102: “for a bandwidth of 1 Hz, NEP = \(2hc/\lambda\)” is correct numerically, but the NEP of an ideal (quantum-noise-limited) detector grows as \(\sqrt B\); NEP is bandwidth-independent only when the noise does not depend on the signal (Chapter 10, warning box).
Slide 105: “Noise from load: \(4k_BT/R_L\) = 1.29 nA” should read \([4k_BTB/R_L]^{1/2}=1.29\) nA.
Slides 106–107: the thermal noise of the load is neglected. With a 50 Ω load at 700 MHz it is 0.48 µA rms, and about 9 times more optical power (0.2 µW) is needed for SNR = 10 (Chapter 11). Worth a sentence on the slide, since it is the reason APDs exist.
Slides 133–135: the I–V curve of the 16 Ω example corresponds to an ideality factor η ≈ 2; the optimum load is 15.5 Ω and the true FF 0.727 (the slide’s 0.72 assumes the 16 Ω point is the MPP, which is very nearly true) (Chapter 13).
Slide 149: NEP is printed “W Hz” (W Hz⁻¹ᐟ²). Slide 150: “0.95 W/A” should be A/W.
Slide 130: the a-Si:H efficiency recomputed from \(V_{oc}J_{sc}\)FF is 9.9 % (slide 10.1 %, rounding in the source table).
Missing material added as “Going further”: transit-time frequency response and the transit/RC optimum (Chapter 2, Chapter 5), McIntyre excess noise and the optimum APD gain (Chapter 11), internal photoemission and MSM capacitance (Chapter 7), gain–bandwidth of photoconductors and phototransistors, lock-in detection, photon transfer curve, receiver sensitivity and BER (Chapter 14), and the Shockley–Queisser limit (Chapter 15).
